title: (1955) Grandma's Money-Saving Tricks Nobody Uses Anymore

scenes.text: Your grandmother never threw anything away. You probably noticed it as a child. The drawer full of rubber bands. The coffee cans of buttons. The bread bags folded into neat little squares. It may have seemed odd back then. But every one of those habits had a reason, and most of them saved her family real money.
scenes.caption: SHE NEVER THREW ANYTHING AWAY

scenes.text: The women who ran American homes in nineteen fifty-five had grown up in the Great Depression and lived through the rationing of the war. They knew what it was to have nothing. So even when times got better, they kept the habits. And they could stretch one paycheck further than anyone alive today.
scenes.caption: SHE REMEMBERED THE DEPRESSION

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-five, the typical family earned a little over four thousand dollars a year. Food took a much bigger share of that money than it does today. So every penny saved in the kitchen was a penny that could go toward the mortgage, the car payment, or the children's shoes.
scenes.caption: EVERY PENNY COUNTED

scenes.text: Tonight, let's open grandma's kitchen drawers and go through her tricks, one by one. Twenty-one money-saving habits from nineteen fifty-five that almost nobody uses anymore. Some of them are funny. Some are brilliant. And a few might be worth bringing back.
scenes.caption: 21 FORGOTTEN TRICKS

scenes.text: Number one. The bacon grease can. Next to every stove sat a tin can or a little crock with a strainer on top. Every drop of bacon fat went into it. Grandma used it to fry eggs, to season green beans, to make cornbread, and to grease the pans. Nobody bought shortening for frying when the bacon grease was free.
scenes.caption: 1. THE BACON GREASE CAN

scenes.text: Number two. One chicken, three meals. On Sunday, a roast chicken for dinner. On Monday, the leftover meat became chicken salad or creamed chicken on toast. And on Tuesday, the bones and the scraps went into a pot with an onion and some carrots, and simmered all afternoon into soup.
scenes.caption: 2. ONE CHICKEN, THREE MEALS

scenes.text: Number three. Stale bread was never thrown out. It became bread pudding with raisins and a little cinnamon. Or French toast on Saturday morning. Or breadcrumbs for the meatloaf, dried in a slow oven and crushed with a rolling pin. In a careful kitchen, nothing went to waste.
scenes.caption: 3. NEVER WASTE BREAD

scenes.text: Leftovers had a schedule all their own. Sunday's roast became Monday's hash and Wednesday's stew. Leftover mashed potatoes became potato cakes, fried in that same bacon grease. A spoonful of peas went into the soup pot. The refrigerator was full of little glass dishes with lids, each holding something waiting for its second chance.
scenes.caption: LEFTOVER NIGHT

scenes.text: Number four. Meatloaf stretched with oatmeal or crackers. A pound of ground beef could feed a family of six if you mixed in enough bread crumbs, oats and a little milk. Grandma's meatloaf may have been more cracker than meat. But with a stripe of ketchup across the top, nobody complained.
scenes.caption: 4. STRETCH THE MEAT

scenes.text: Number five. The vegetable garden and the canning jars. In the summer, grandma grew tomatoes, beans, cucumbers and squash. In August, the kitchen turned into a steam bath as she put up dozens of Mason jars, lined up on basement shelves like jewels. Peaches, pickles, tomatoes, jam. Enough to last the whole winter.
scenes.caption: 5. PUT IT UP FOR WINTER

scenes.text: Canning day was often a family affair. The children washed the jars and snapped the beans on the back porch. Grandma worked the big pot on the stove. And all evening, the kitchen was full of little pinging sounds, as the lids sealed one by one. Every ping meant one more jar safe for the winter.
scenes.caption: THE PING OF THE LIDS

scenes.text: Number six. Powdered milk mixed in with the real thing. Lots of families quietly mixed a pitcher of powdered milk into the fresh milk to make it go further. The children noticed the taste. The mothers pretended they didn't know what they were talking about.
scenes.caption: 6. THE POWDERED MILK TRICK

scenes.text: Number seven. Nothing was disposable. Aluminum foil was washed, smoothed flat and used again. Glass jars became drinking glasses and storage containers. Bread bags held sandwiches. Paper grocery sacks became book covers for school, trash bags, and wrapping for packages. Even string was wound into a ball and saved.
scenes.caption: 7. NOTHING WAS DISPOSABLE

scenes.text: Number eight. The button jar. Before an old shirt became a rag, grandma cut off every button and dropped it into a jar. When a button popped off a coat, she didn't buy a new one. She poured the jar onto the table and found a match. Children loved sorting through that jar on rainy afternoons.
scenes.caption: 8. THE BUTTON JAR

scenes.text: Number nine. The rag bag. Worn-out clothes were never thrown away. They went into a cloth bag hanging on the back of a door. Old towels became dust cloths. Old sheets became bandages and dish towels. Old wool became braided rugs. Old dresses became quilts, pieced together by hand over a whole winter.
scenes.caption: 9. THE RAG BAG

scenes.text: Quilting was also how women got together. A quilting bee in the church basement or somebody's living room, a dozen women around a wooden frame, stitching and talking for hours. They finished a quilt in a day, and the best gossip in town was shared over those stitches.
scenes.caption: THE QUILTING BEE

scenes.text: Number ten. Mending, darning and patching. Grandma kept a wooden darning egg in her sewing basket. When a sock wore through at the heel, she slipped it over the egg and wove a new heel with needle and thread. Elbows got patches. Collars were turned inside out to hide the wear. Clothes lasted for years.
scenes.caption: 10. THE DARNING EGG

scenes.text: Number eleven. Sewing the family's clothes at home. Many women sewed their own dresses and their children's clothes on a treadle or electric machine. They bought patterns at the five-and-dime for a quarter. And some flour and feed sacks came printed with flowers and checks, so farm women could turn them into dresses and aprons.
scenes.caption: 11. FEED SACK DRESSES

scenes.text: Number twelve. Hand-me-downs, all the way down. The oldest child got the new coat. Two years later, it went to the next child. Then the next. By the time it reached the youngest, it had been let out, taken in, patched and re-hemmed three times. And cousins traded boxes of outgrown clothes at every family visit.
scenes.caption: 12. HAND-ME-DOWNS

scenes.text: Shoes were resoled, not replaced. The cobbler downtown put new heels and soles on the same pair of shoes again and again. Children's shoes were bought a size too big, stuffed with tissue in the toe, and grown into. And every Saturday night, fathers polished the whole family's shoes for church.
scenes.caption: THE COBBLER

scenes.text: Number thirteen. Turning off the lights. If you left a room with the light on, you heard about it. Grandpa walked through the house every evening, switching off lamps behind everyone. Do you think we own the electric company? Every child in America heard that sentence at least once.
scenes.query: 1950s man turning off lamp living room
scenes.caption: 13. WHO OWNS THE ELECTRIC COMPANY?

scenes.text: Number fourteen. Hanging the laundry outside. Even families with a new electric dryer often hung their wash on the line in good weather, because sunshine was free. Sheets dried stiff and smelled like fresh air. And wooden clothespins lasted for decades, kept in a cloth bag hung right on the line.
scenes.caption: 14. SUNSHINE WAS FREE

scenes.text: Number fifteen. Homemade cleaning supplies. Vinegar and water for the windows, wiped with crumpled newspaper so there were no streaks. Baking soda for the sink and the oven. Lemon juice for stains. A bar of plain soap for nearly everything else. One box of baking soda could clean half the house.
scenes.caption: 15. VINEGAR AND NEWSPAPER

scenes.text: Haircuts happened at home too. Many mothers cut the children's hair at the kitchen table, with a towel around the neck and a bowl as a guide. The results were not always beautiful. But a barber cost money, and a bowl was free. Every family album has at least one photograph to prove it.
scenes.caption: THE BOWL CUT

scenes.text: Number sixteen. Making do with one of everything. One bathroom. One telephone. One radio, and later one television. One car. Most families didn't feel deprived. It was simply how everybody lived, and the money that wasn't spent on extras went into the savings account at the bank.
scenes.caption: 16. ONE OF EVERYTHING

scenes.text: Number seventeen. The coin purse and cash only. Grandma paid for almost everything in cash. If she didn't have the money, she didn't buy the thing. Credit cards hardly existed in nineteen fifty-five. When people did buy on credit, it was usually a big item from a store that knew them, and they paid it off as fast as they could.
scenes.caption: 17. CASH ONLY

scenes.text: Number eighteen. The layaway plan. If you wanted a winter coat or a bicycle for Christmas, the store put it aside for you behind the counter. You paid a little every week until it was paid in full, and only then did you take it home. No interest. No debt. Just patience.
scenes.caption: 18. LAYAWAY

scenes.text: The Christmas club worked the same way. In January, you opened a special account at the bank and put in fifty cents or a dollar every week. In late November, the bank mailed you a check for the whole amount. That check paid for Christmas, and nobody started the new year in debt.
scenes.caption: THE CHRISTMAS CLUB

scenes.text: Number nineteen. Trading stamps. Every purchase at the supermarket or the gas station came with little stamps. Green ones, or gold ones, or blue ones. Grandma saved them in a drawer, and on a rainy afternoon the children licked them and pasted them into booklets. A few dozen books might buy a toaster, a lamp or a set of dishes.
scenes.caption: 19. LICKING THE STAMPS

scenes.text: Number twenty. Coupons and the Wednesday newspaper. Grocery stores published their weekly specials in the newspaper, often on Wednesday or Thursday. Grandma read the ads with a pencil, planned the week's meals around what was on sale, and sometimes went to two or three different stores to get the best price on each item.
scenes.caption: 20. THE WEEKLY SPECIALS

scenes.text: And grandma knew her grocer. If she bought a little extra flour when it was cheap, he might set aside the bruised apples for her pies at half price. If the family hit a hard month, many corner grocers ran a tab, written in a little notebook behind the counter, and trusted her to pay it off when she could.
scenes.caption: THE GROCER'S NOTEBOOK

scenes.text: And number twenty-one. The cookie tin that never held cookies. Every grandmother had one. A round blue tin that looked like it was full of butter cookies. Inside, it held thread, needles, buttons and pins. Or sometimes, tucked at the very bottom, a few folded bills saved for an emergency. You never knew until you opened it.
scenes.caption: 21. THE COOKIE TIN

scenes.text: It's easy to laugh at some of these habits now. But think about what they added up to. A family of five, living on one modest paycheck, owning their home, with money in the bank and food on the shelves for the winter. That didn't happen by accident. It happened because somebody in that house was very, very good at it.
scenes.caption: IT DIDN'T HAPPEN BY ACCIDENT

scenes.text: Those women never called it budgeting, or saving the planet, or reducing waste. They called it common sense. Use it up, wear it out, make it do, or do without. That old saying hung in a lot of American kitchens, sometimes stitched on a sampler on the wall.
scenes.caption: USE IT UP, WEAR IT OUT

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. Which of these did your mother or grandmother do? And did we miss one? We read every comment, and we'd love to hear the trick your family swore by. And stay with us, because next we're going to a nineteen fifty-five factory town. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHICH ONE DID YOUR GRANDMA DO?
